22:0422 Minuten, 4 SekundenFabritzio Benadetti, the Italian neuroscientist who showed up earlier in our story with his Nlloxxone
22:1222 Minuten, 12 Sekundenexperiments, has spent decades trying to map exactly what happens in the brain and body when a placebo is administered.
22:2022 Minuten, 20 SekundenAnd one of his most important contributions is showing that the placebo effect is not one thing. It's
22:2822 Minuten, 28 Sekundenseveral different mechanisms that happen to get lumped under the same word. for pain. As we talked about, the mechanism
22:3622 Minuten, 36 Sekundeninvolves the release of endogenous opioids, your body's own painkillers.
22:4222 Minuten, 42 SekundenBenedetti proved this by showing that the opioid blocker nlloxxone could shut down placebo analesia.
22:4922 Minuten, 49 SekundenBut that's only one pathway. For Parkinson's disease, the mechanism is different. Benadeti and his colleagues
22:5722 Minuten, 57 Sekundenshowed that when Parkinson's patients were given a placebo, they believed was their medication, their brains actually
23:0423 Minuten, 4 Sekundenreleased dopamine in the striatum. The part of the brain where dopamine is depleted in Parkinson's,
23:1123 Minuten, 11 Sekundennot a metaphorical release, actual measurable dopamine detected by PET scans. The expectation of receiving
23:2123 Minuten, 21 Sekundenmedication triggered the very neurochemical the medication was designed to replace. And this is genuinely strange if you sit with it.
23:3023 Minuten, 30 SekundenThe brain anticipating that it's about to receive a drug starts producing some of what that drug would have delivered.
23:3823 Minuten, 38 SekundenNot all of it, not reliably enough to replace the drug, but enough to create a real, if temporary, change in symptoms.
23:4823 Minuten, 48 SekundenIt's as if the body has learned through years of taking a medication and feeling better afterward that the ritual of
23:5523 Minuten, 55 Sekundentaking the pill is a signal to start the process early, which if you think about it is just classical conditioning.
24:0524 Minuten, 5 SekundenPavlov's dogs salivated at the sound of a bell because the bell had been paired with food. Your nervous system releases
24:1324 Minuten, 13 Sekundendopamine at the sight of a pill because the pill has been paired with dopamine replacement. The mechanism is ancient.
24:2224 Minuten, 22 SekundenIt's the same basic learning system that every animal with a nervous system uses to predict what's coming next and prepare for it.
24:3224 Minuten, 32 SekundenRobert Ader, a psychologist at the University of Rochester, actually demonstrated this connection between
24:3924 Minuten, 39 Sekundenconditioning and immune function back in the 1970s in an experiment that was at the time considered almost heretical.
24:4924 Minuten, 49 SekundenAder was working with rats, pairing a distinctively flavored water, saccharine sweetened, with an injection of
24:5724 Minuten, 57 Sekundencyclophosphomide, a drug that suppresses the immune system.
25:0225 Minuten, 2 SekundenAfter several pairings, he gave the rats just the sweetened water, no drug, and
25:0925 Minuten, 9 Sekundentheir immune systems suppressed. Anyway, the taste alone was enough to trigger the physiological response that the drug
25:1625 Minuten, 16 Sekundenhad originally caused. Ader called this conditioned immunosuppression and it was one of the founding experiments of a field that came to be
25:2525 Minuten, 25 Sekundenknown as psychonuroimmunology which is exactly as complicated as it sounds but boils down to a simple and
25:3325 Minuten, 33 Sekundenprofound idea. The nervous system, the endocrine system and the immune system are not separate departments.
25:4325 Minuten, 43 SekundenThey talk to each other constantly and the brain sitting at the top of that conversation can influence the body's
25:5025 Minuten, 50 Sekundenimmune responses through learned associations.
25:5525 Minuten, 55 SekundenYou've probably experienced a mild version of this yourself, even if you've never thought of it in these terms. If
26:0226 Minuten, 2 Sekundenyou've ever felt nauseous walking into a hospital because of a bad experience you had there years ago, that's your body
26:0926 Minuten, 9 Sekundenresponding to contextual cues. the smell, the lighting, the particular quality of the air with a physiological
26:1826 Minuten, 18 Sekundenreaction that was originally triggered by something else entirely.
26:2226 Minuten, 22 SekundenYour body learned that those cues predict a certain kind of experience and it started preparing for that experience
26:3026 Minuten, 30 Sekundenbefore anything actually happened. The placebo effect runs on the same rails just in the other direction.
Kapitel 8: Limits of the effect
26:3826 Minuten, 38 SekundenInstead of the context predicting something unpleasant and the body bracing for it, the context predicts healing and the body begins to mobilize toward it.
26:4926 Minuten, 49 SekundenBut here's where it gets genuinely tricky and where a lot of the popular accounts of the placebo effect start to come apart.
26:5726 Minuten, 57 SekundenBecause there are limits and the limits are important and being honest about them is actually more interesting than pretending they don't exist.
27:0627 Minuten, 6 SekundenPlaceos are strongest for subjective outcomes, things the patient reports.
27:1227 Minuten, 12 SekundenPain, nausea, fatigue, mood, anxiety, the perception of how well you can move
27:1927 Minuten, 19 Sekundenor breathe. These are real experiences and the improvements are real improvements, but they are experiences
27:2627 Minuten, 26 Sekundenthat are by their nature shaped by expectation and attention.
27:3327 Minuten, 33 SekundenWhen you move to objective measurable outcomes, things like tumor size, viral load, bone density, blood sugar levels,
27:4327 Minuten, 43 Sekundenthe placebo effect gets much, much smaller. In many cases, it effectively disappears. This doesn't mean the
27:5127 Minuten, 51 Sekundenplacebo effect is just in your head in the dismissive sense people sometimes mean by that phrase. Pain is in your
28:0028 Minutenhead and pain is one of the most debilitating things a human being can experience. Nausea is in your head and
28:0828 Minuten, 8 Sekundennausea can make a person unable to eat, work or function.
28:1328 Minuten, 13 SekundenThe fact that placeos work primarily on subjective experience doesn't make them trivial. But it does mean that the
28:2028 Minuten, 20 Sekundenplacebo effect is not going to shrink a tumor or cure an infection. And anyone who tells you otherwise is selling
28:2728 Minuten, 27 Sekundensomething. The body's expectationdriven healing systems are real and powerful, but they operate within specific
28:3628 Minuten, 36 Sekundenchannels, mostly the channels that regulate pain perception, stress hormones, neurotransmitter release, and immune modulation.
28:4728 Minuten, 47 SekundenThey are not magic. and treating them as magic actually makes it harder to use them well. Which brings up something
28:5528 Minuten, 55 Sekundenthat the researchers in this field have been wrestling with for decades now.
29:0029 MinutenSomething that sounds like a simple ethical question but turns out to be anything but simple. If placeos work,
29:0729 Minuten, 7 Sekundenand they do, and if the mechanism is real, and it is, then is it ethical to use them? Can a doctor give a patient a sugar pill and tell them it's medicine?
29:2029 Minuten, 20 Sekundenshould they? And if honesty matters, which it does, then how do you harness the placebo effect without lying to the
29:2829 Minuten, 28 Sekundenperson you're trying to help? That tension between the power of the effect and the ethics of deception has shaped
29:3529 Minuten, 35 Sekundenalmost everything about how modern medicine thinks about placeos.
Kapitel 9: The ethics of open-label
29:4029 Minuten, 40 SekundenAnd the answer that started emerging in the early 2010s from a researcher at Harvard named Ted Capchuk was stranger
29:4929 Minuten, 49 Sekundenand more hopeful than almost anyone expected. Because what Capchuk wanted to know was whether you could strip away
29:5629 Minuten, 56 Sekundenthe deception entirely, tell a patient exactly what they were getting, hand them a bottle clearly
30:0430 Minuten, 4 Sekundenlabeled placebo, and still see the effect work. And the answer against almost every intuition you might have about how this should go was yes.
30:1630 Minuten, 16 SekundenLet that settle for a moment because it really is one of the strangest findings in this whole story.
30:2430 Minuten, 24 SekundenThe placebo effect, the thing that was defined for most of its history by the idea that the patient doesn't know, the
30:3230 Minuten, 32 Sekundenthing whose very power seemed to depend on a lie, turns out to work even when you tell the truth. Not always, not for
30:4130 Minuten, 41 Sekundeneverything, but reliably enough and strongly enough that it has forced a genuine rethinking of what the effect actually is.
30:5030 Minuten, 50 SekundenCapchuk's first big openlel trial was published in 2010 and the condition he chose was irritable bowel syndrome which
31:0031 Minutenis a good test case because IBS involves a lot of subjective suffering a lot of pain and discomfort that is genuinely
31:0831 Minuten, 8 Sekundenexperienced but hard to measure from the outside and it's a condition where the placebo response in clinical trials has
31:1631 Minuten, 16 Sekundenalways been unusually large. He took 80 patients with IBS and split them into
31:2331 Minuten, 23 Sekundentwo groups. One group got no treatment at all, just continued with whatever they were already doing. The other group was given a bottle of pills.
31:3431 Minuten, 34 SekundenAnd here's the part that matters. They were told clearly and explicitly that the pills contained no active ingredient.
31:4431 Minuten, 44 SekundenThe bottle was labeled placebo pills.
31:4831 Minuten, 48 SekundenThe researchers explained to the patients that placeos have been shown in clinical studies to produce significant
31:5431 Minuten, 54 Sekundenimprovement in IBS symptoms through mindbody self-healing processes.
32:0032 MinutenThat was the framing, no deception, no ambiguity.
32:0632 Minuten, 6 SekundenYou are taking a sugar pill and here is why we think it might help. Anyway, after 3 weeks, the group taking the open
32:1432 Minuten, 14 Sekundenlabel placeos reported significantly more symptom relief than the no treatment group. Not a subtle difference
32:2232 Minuten, 22 Sekundeneither. The improvement was comparable to what you'd typically see with the best available IBS medications at the
32:2932 Minuten, 29 Sekundentime. People who knew they were swallowing inert pills, who had been told in plain language that the pills
32:3632 Minuten, 36 Sekundenwere inert, got better anyway. Their pain decreased, their symptom severity dropped, their quality of life improved.
32:4632 Minuten, 46 SekundenNow, you might be thinking that this has to be some kind of trick, that maybe the patients didn't really believe the pills were inert or that they convinced
32:5432 Minuten, 54 Sekundenthemselves there was a secret ingredient or that the researchers winked when they said the word placebo.
33:0333 Minuten, 3 SekundenCapchuk anticipated all of that. The disclosure was thorough and unambiguous.
33:1033 Minuten, 10 SekundenPatients were told multiple times, and follow-up interviews confirmed that the patients understood perfectly well what
33:1833 Minuten, 18 Sekundenthey were taking. They just got better anyway. So, how do you explain that? If
33:2533 Minuten, 25 Sekundenthe placebo effect is about expectation, and if the patient knows there's nothing in the pill, where is the expectation
33:3333 Minuten, 33 Sekundencoming from? This is where you have to update your model of what expectation actually means in this context. Because
33:4233 Minuten, 42 Sekundenit turns out that conscious explicit belief, the kind you could put into words if someone asked you, is only one
33:5133 Minuten, 51 Sekundenlayer of the system. Below that, there are older, less verbal processes at work.
33:5933 Minuten, 59 SekundenThe act of taking a pill is itself a signal. Your body has spent a lifetime learning that pills are associated with
34:0634 Minuten, 6 Sekundenfeeling better. You take a pill, something shifts.
34:1134 Minuten, 11 SekundenNot because you've reasoned your way to a conclusion, but because the ritual, the physical act, the context of receiving care from a medical
34:2034 Minuten, 20 Sekundenprofessional. All of it activates conditioned responses that operate below the level of conscious belief.
34:2834 Minuten, 28 SekundenThink about rats for a second. The ones who learned to suppress their own immune systems when they tasted saccharine.
34:3734 Minuten, 37 SekundenNobody told those rats that saccharine was an immunosuppressant.
34:4134 Minuten, 41 SekundenThey didn't believe it. They didn't have beliefs in the way we usually mean that word.
34:4834 Minuten, 48 SekundenTheir bodies simply learned an association. And the association drove a real physiological change.
34:5534 Minuten, 55 SekundenSomething similar seems to be happening with open label placeos in humans except we have the added layer of language of
35:0335 Minuten, 3 Sekundenbeing told that this process exists of being given a framework for understanding why a sugar pill might
35:1135 Minuten, 11 Sekundenactually do something. That framework isn't a lie. It's a simplified but basically accurate description of how
35:1935 Minuten, 19 Sekundenconditioned healing responses work. And giving someone that framework seems to be enough to let the machinery run.
35:2735 Minuten, 27 SekundenCapchuk has talked about this in terms of what he calls the therapeutic encounter, which is a broader idea than
Kapitel 10: The therapeutic alliance
35:3335 Minuten, 33 Sekundenjust the pill. The encounter includes everything. The act of going to see someone about your problem, being
35:4135 Minuten, 41 Sekundenlistened to, being examined, being given something to take, even if that something is openly inert.
35:5135 Minuten, 51 Sekundenbeing told that your body has the capacity to respond.
35:5635 Minuten, 56 SekundenAll of these elements carry information and the body reads that information the way it reads any other environmental
36:0336 Minuten, 3 Sekundensignal through pathways that don't require conscious endorsement to function. You don't have to believe in
36:1036 Minuten, 10 Sekundengravity for it to work on you. And you don't have to believe in the placebo effect for it to work on you either.
36:1736 Minuten, 17 SekundenThough believing probably helps at the margins since that first IBS study, open label placebo research has expanded
36:2536 Minuten, 25 Sekundenconsiderably. Claudia Carvalo working with Capchuk published a trial in 2016
36:3336 Minuten, 33 Sekundenlooking at chronic lower back pain, one of the most common and most stubbornly treatment resistant conditions in
36:4036 Minuten, 40 Sekundenmedicine. Patients who added open label placeos to their usual treatment reported significantly greater pain
36:4836 Minuten, 48 Sekundenreduction than those who continued with treatment alone. Again, no deception.
36:5536 Minuten, 55 SekundenAgain, real improvement. Other groups have run openle label placebo studies on cancer related fatigue on allergic
37:0337 Minuten, 3 Sekundenrhinitis on test anxiety and the results while not uniform have been surprisingly
37:1137 Minuten, 11 Sekundenconsistent. The effects tend to be moderate not miraculous but they show up and they show up in conditions where any
37:1937 Minuten, 19 Sekundenimprovement matters enormously to the person experiencing it. And this is where the ethical knot starts to loosen
37:2737 Minuten, 27 Sekundenat least a little. Because the old dilemma, the one that kept doctors from using placeos honestly, was that you had
37:3537 Minuten, 35 Sekundento lie for them to work. If you told the truth, you'd break the spell.
37:4237 Minuten, 42 SekundenOpenle label placeos suggest that the spell was never really about the lie. It was about the ritual, the context, the
37:5037 Minuten, 50 Sekundenrelationship, the embodied learning that happens when a person in distress receives care in a structured, attentive
37:5737 Minuten, 57 Sekundenway. The lie was a shortcut to activating those processes. But it turns out there are other shortcuts, ones that don't require anyone to be deceived.
38:0938 Minuten, 9 SekundenThat said, and this is important, the open label placebo story is still young.
38:1638 Minuten, 16 SekundenThe studies are generally small. The conditions studied are mostly ones where subjective symptoms dominate. And
38:2438 Minuten, 24 Sekundenthere's a real question about how much of the effect comes from the novelty of the approach, from the extra attention
38:3338 Minuten, 33 Sekundenand explanation that patients in these studies receive. from the simple fact that someone is spending 20 minutes
38:4138 Minuten, 41 Sekundentelling you about how your body's healing systems work, which is itself a form of care that most medical
38:4838 Minuten, 48 Sekundenencounters don't include. Separating the pill from the encounter is genuinely difficult. And some researchers have
38:5638 Minuten, 56 Sekundenargued that what Capchuk is really studying isn't the open label pill at all, but the enhanced therapeutic
39:0339 Minuten, 3 Sekundenrelationship that surrounds it. Capchuk himself would probably say that's not a criticism.
39:1139 Minuten, 11 SekundenIt's the point. He's been arguing for years that the placebo effect was never really about the placebo.
39:1939 Minuten, 19 SekundenIt was about everything around the placebo. The warmth of the clinician, the confidence in the explanation, the
39:2739 Minuten, 27 Sekundenphysical environment, the degree to which the patient feels heard. In a series of elegant studies, he's tried to pull these components apart.
39:3839 Minuten, 38 SekundenOne of the most striking was a trial involving patients with IBS published in 2008 where he compared three conditions.
39:4739 Minuten, 47 SekundenOne group was put on a waiting list, no treatment at all. A second group received sham acupuncture needles placed
39:5639 Minuten, 56 Sekundenat non-acupuncture points delivered by a practitioner who was polite but business-like who didn't engage in much
40:0340 Minuten, 3 Sekundenconversation. A third group received the same sham acupuncture but from a practitioner who was warm, empathetic,
40:1240 Minuten, 12 Sekundenwho asked about their symptoms in detail, who expressed confidence and concern.
40:1840 Minuten, 18 SekundenAll three groups knew they might be receiving a sham treatment. The results were graded like a staircase. The waiting list group improved the least.
40:2840 Minuten, 28 SekundenThe limited interaction sham group improved more. And the augmented interaction sham group, the one where
40:3640 Minuten, 36 Sekundenthe practitioner was warm and attentive, improved the most, reaching levels of symptom relief that matched what you'd see with actual IBS medication.
40:4640 Minuten, 46 SekundenThink about what that means. The same inert treatment delivered by the same type of practitioner in the same
40:5440 Minuten, 54 Sekundenclinical setting produced dramatically different results depending on how much warmth and attention came with it. The
41:0141 Minuten, 1 Sekundepill or in this case the needle was almost beside the point. What mattered was the quality of the human interaction
41:0941 Minuten, 9 Sekundensurrounding it. You've almost certainly experienced some version of this yourself.
41:1641 Minuten, 16 SekundenThink about a time you went to see a doctor who really listened, who took your concerns seriously, who explained what was happening in a way that made you feel understood.
41:2841 Minuten, 28 SekundenAnd compare that with a time you saw someone rushed, distracted, someone who barely looked up from their screen.
41:3641 Minuten, 36 SekundenEven if the diagnosis and the prescription were identical, the two experiences felt completely different.
41:4441 Minuten, 44 SekundenAnd there's good reason to think they produce different outcomes.
41:4841 Minuten, 48 SekundenNot because one doctor was better at medicine in the narrow pharmacological sense, but because the context in which
41:5641 Minuten, 56 Sekundenthe medicine was delivered carried its own therapeutic signal.
42:0142 Minuten, 1 SekundeThis is the part of the placebo story that starts to feel less like a quirk of clinical trials and more like something
42:0842 Minuten, 8 Sekundenfundamental about how healing works in social animals. We are creatures who regulate each other. A calm voice lowers
42:1742 Minuten, 17 Sekundenanother person's cortisol. A trusted presence changes how pain is processed.
42:2442 Minuten, 24 SekundenThe knowledge that someone competent is paying attention to your problem changes the neurochemical environment in which
42:3142 Minuten, 31 Sekundenyour body responds to that problem. None of this is mystical. It's the predictable behavior of a nervous system
42:3942 Minuten, 39 Sekundenthat evolved in groups that learned over millions of years to use social signals as information about safety and that adjusts its internal state accordingly.
Kapitel 11: Optimizing delivery systems
42:5042 Minuten, 50 SekundenAnd this is where the placebo story starts to merge with something much larger. something that touches the way
42:5742 Minuten, 57 Sekundenwe design hospitals, train doctors, structure clinical encounters, and think about what medicine actually
43:0643 Minuten, 6 Sekundenis. Because if a significant portion of the healing that happens in a medical context comes not from the drug, but
43:1443 Minuten, 14 Sekundenfrom everything around the drug, then everything around the drug matters.
43:2043 Minuten, 20 SekundenThe color of the pill matters. The confidence of the doctor matters. The ritual of the prescription matters. The time spent listening matters.
43:3143 Minuten, 31 SekundenAnd in a medical system that is increasingly squeezed for time, that replaces 15-minute consultations with
43:3943 Minuten, 39 Sekunden7-inute ones that roots patients through algorithms and screens rather than conversations.
43:4643 Minuten, 46 SekundenYou have to wonder how much of the placebo effect the good real physiologically measurable part of it is being quietly lost.
43:5843 Minuten, 58 SekundenFabitio Benadeti the neuroscientist whose nlloxxone work we talked about earlier has done some of the most unsettling research on this question.
44:0844 Minuten, 8 SekundenHe's shown that when you remove the human context entirely, when you administer a painkiller through a hidden
44:1544 Minuten, 15 Sekundenintravenous drip, so the patient doesn't know they're receiving it, the drug still works, but it works significantly
44:2344 Minuten, 23 Sekundenless well than when the same drug is given openly by a person in a way the patient can see and understand.
44:3244 Minuten, 32 SekundenThe drug's pharmacological effect is still there, but the boost that comes from knowing you're being treated, from
44:3944 Minuten, 39 Sekundenseeing the clinician, from the whole ritual of care, that boost disappears.
44:4644 Minuten, 46 SekundenBenedetti calls this the open hidden paradigm and it suggests that a meaningful fraction of what we attribute
44:5444 Minuten, 54 Sekundento our best drugs is actually coming from the context in which those drugs are delivered.
45:0145 Minuten, 1 SekundeWhich raises a question that almost nobody in medicine is comfortable asking out loud. A question about what happens
45:0945 Minuten, 9 Sekundenwhen you start optimizing not just the molecule but the delivery context itself. And that's exactly what some
45:1645 Minuten, 16 Sekundenresearchers have started doing quietly without much fanfare in ways that most patients never notice. Think about the
45:2545 Minuten, 25 Sekundenlast time you took a pill. Not the swallowing of it, but everything before that. The doctor's tone when she told
45:3345 Minuten, 33 Sekundenyou what it was for. Whether she seemed confident or hedging. Whether she said
45:3945 Minuten, 39 Sekundenthis should help, or we can try this and see. Whether she looked at you when she said it, or whether she was already
45:4845 Minuten, 48 Sekundentyping into the screen. The feel of the pharmacy bag in your hand, the weight of the bottle, the color of the capsule,
45:5745 Minuten, 57 Sekundenwhether anyone explained what to expect or whether you were handed a print out and sent on your way. All of that, every
46:0546 Minuten, 5 Sekundensingle piece of it is part of the treatment.
46:0946 Minuten, 9 Sekundennot metaphorically, pharmacologically, because your brain is already responding to those cues before the active
46:1846 Minuten, 18 Sekundeningredient has dissolved in your stomach. And here's what's genuinely interesting about where this research has gone. It's not just that context
46:2746 Minuten, 27 Sekundenhelps, it's that the absence of context actively hurts. Strip away the human elements, the eye contact, the
46:3546 Minuten, 35 Sekundenreassurance, the sense that someone competent is paying attention to you specifically, and you don't just lose
46:4346 Minuten, 43 Sekundenthe placebo boost. You sometimes lose a measurable chunk of the drug's apparent effectiveness. The molecule does what
46:5046 Minuten, 50 Sekundenthe molecule does, but the body's own response to the molecule, the way it primes itself to receive help. The
46:5746 Minuten, 57 Sekundenneurochemical anticipation that Benadeti has mapped so carefully, that part needs a signal. It needs a reason to fire. And
47:0647 Minuten, 6 Sekundenin a system that is moving faster and faster, that signal is getting thinner and thinner. There's a term for this
47:1447 Minuten, 14 Sekundenthat you might have come across, though it's more common in medical ethics than in neuroscience. It's called the therapeutic alliance.
47:2247 Minuten, 22 SekundenOriginally, it comes from psychotherapy, where it refers to the relationship between therapist and client, the sense of trust, shared goals, mutual respect.
47:3547 Minuten, 35 SekundenBut it applies just as powerfully in general medicine. And the data behind it is surprisingly strong. A metaanalysis
47:4347 Minuten, 43 Sekundenpublished in 2014 by John Kelly and colleagues at Harvard drawing on dozens of studies across multiple medical
47:5047 Minuten, 50 Sekundenspecialties found that the quality of the doctor patient relationship was a significant predictor of health outcomes.
47:5847 Minuten, 58 SekundenNot just patient satisfaction, not just whether people felt heard, but actual clinical outcomes, pain levels,
48:0748 Minuten, 7 Sekundenrecovery times, symptom severity, the effect size was comparable to some widely prescribed treatments. Which
48:1548 Minuten, 15 Sekundenmeans that the relationship itself, the warmth, the attentiveness, the communication functions as a kind of
48:2348 Minuten, 23 Sekundenmedicine. And like any medicine, when you reduce the dose, the effect shrinks.
48:3048 Minuten, 30 SekundenNow, you might be thinking, "Sure, but doctors have always known that bedside manner matters." That's not news. And
48:3948 Minuten, 39 Sekundenyou'd be right that it's not new as an intuition. What's new is the mechanistic understanding of why it matters. the
48:4748 Minuten, 47 Sekundenneurochemical evidence that Benadeti and Capchuk and others have assembled showing that this isn't just about
48:5448 Minuten, 54 Sekundenfeelings. It's about endogenous opioids being released or not released. Dopamine systems activating or staying quiet.
49:0449 Minuten, 4 SekundenStress hormones like cortisol dropping or remaining elevated.
49:0949 Minuten, 9 SekundenThe therapeutic alliance isn't a nice extra on top of real medicine.
49:1549 Minuten, 15 SekundenIt's part of the biological pathway through which medicine works. And that changes the conversation because now
49:2349 Minuten, 23 Sekundenyou're not asking doctors to be nicer as a courtesy. You're asking them to be attentive as a clinical intervention.
49:3049 Minuten, 30 SekundenCapchuk, the researcher whose open label work we spent time with earlier, has been particularly sharp on this point.
49:3849 Minuten, 38 SekundenIn his 2008 study, the one where he decomposed the clinical encounter into layers, what he demonstrated wasn't just
49:4649 Minuten, 46 Sekundenthat warmth helps. He showed that it helps in a dose- dependent way.
49:5249 Minuten, 52 SekundenMore warmth, more time, more attentiveness, more clinical improvement, even when the treatment
49:5949 Minuten, 59 Sekundenitself was completely inert. sham acupuncture with a caring practitioner outperformed sham acupuncture with a
50:0850 Minuten, 8 Sekundenbusiness-like one. And both outperformed sitting on a waiting list. The ritual and the relationship were doing heavy
50:1750 Minuten, 17 Sekundenpharmacological lifting. And they were doing it in a way you could measure, graph, and replicate.
Kapitel 12: Structural barriers
50:2450 Minuten, 24 SekundenSo what happens when you take that finding seriously?
50:2850 Minuten, 28 SekundenWhat happens when a health system looks at this evidence and asks, "Okay, how do we build this into the way we deliver
50:3550 Minuten, 35 Sekundencare?" The honest answer is that very little has happened, at least at the
50:4250 Minuten, 42 Sekundenstructural level. And the reasons for that are worth sitting with because they reveal something about the way modern
50:5050 Minuten, 50 Sekundenmedicine thinks about itself. The dominant model, the one that drives funding, training, and institutional
50:5850 Minuten, 58 Sekundendesign, is what you might call the specific effects model. It assumes that the thing that matters is the active
51:0551 Minuten, 5 Sekundeningredient, the molecule, the procedure, the specific intervention.
51:1151 Minuten, 11 SekundenEverything else, the consultation, the waiting room, the follow-up call is overhead. It's logistics. It's the
51:2051 Minuten, 20 Sekundenwrapper, not the gift. And the entire economic structure of health care is built around that assumption. Doctors
51:2851 Minuten, 28 Sekundenare reimbursed for procedures and prescriptions, not for conversations.
51:3351 Minuten, 33 SekundenHospitals are evaluated on throughput and measurable outcomes tied to specific treatments. The 7-minute consultation
51:4251 Minuten, 42 Sekundenexists not because anyone thinks it's ideal, but because the system is optimized for volume, and volume means
51:5051 Minuten, 50 Sekundenmoving patients through the pipeline as efficiently as possible. And this is where the placebo research becomes
51:5751 Minuten, 57 Sekundengenuinely uncomfortable for the people who run these systems.
52:0152 Minuten, 1 SekundeBecause what Benedetti's open hidden paradigm shows, what Capchuk's decomposition study shows, what Kelly's
52:0852 Minuten, 8 Sekundenmetaanalysis on the therapeutic alliance shows is that the rapper is part of the gift.
52:1552 Minuten, 15 SekundenThe conversation is part of the treatment.
52:1952 Minuten, 19 SekundenThe time spent listening is not overhead. It is a delivery mechanism for endogenous neurochemistry that the
52:2752 Minuten, 27 Sekundensystem cannot bottle and cannot bill for. And when you cut that time, when you replace it with screens and
52:3452 Minuten, 34 Sekundenalgorithms and rushed encounters, you are in a very real pharmacological sense
52:4152 Minuten, 41 Sekundenreducing the dose of something that works. There's a lovely and slightly heartbreaking example of this from
52:4852 Minuten, 48 Sekundenprimary care research. In the early 2000s, a group of researchers in the UK looked at consultation length in general
52:5652 Minuten, 56 Sekundenpractice and found that the average face-to-face appointment had dropped to about 7 to 8 minutes.
53:0453 Minuten, 4 SekundenThey compared outcomes for practices that offered longer consultations around 15 minutes and found that
53:1153 Minuten, 11 Sekundenpatients in longer consultations reported better health outcomes, greater satisfaction, and crucially fewer return
53:2053 Minuten, 20 Sekundenvisits. The longer appointment cost more per visit, but potentially saved money overall because patients got better
53:2853 Minuten, 28 Sekundenfaster and came back less often. The system in optimizing for speed had created a kind of false economy.
53:3753 Minuten, 37 SekundenIt was saving minutes and losing medicine. And you've almost certainly felt this yourself, even if you wouldn't
53:4553 Minuten, 45 Sekundenhave described it in these terms. Think about the difference between a doctor who sits down, makes eye contact, and
53:5253 Minuten, 52 Sekundensays, "Tell me what's been going on." and one who stands by the door with a hand on the handle scanning a chart already halfway to the next room.
54:0254 Minuten, 2 SekundenThe information exchanged might be identical. The prescription might be the same, but something in you responds
54:1054 Minuten, 10 Sekundendifferently. Something relaxes or doesn't. Something trusts or doesn't.
54:1754 Minuten, 17 SekundenAnd that something as we now know has downstream effects on your neurotransmitters, your immune function,
54:2454 Minuten, 24 Sekundenyour pain perception, your recovery trajectory. You're not imagining the difference. Your brain is computing it
54:3254 Minuten, 32 Sekundenbelow the level of conscious awareness and adjusting its response accordingly.
54:3954 Minuten, 39 SekundenThis is where Benadetti's work connects to something even broader, something about the nature of healing environments themselves.
54:4754 Minuten, 47 SekundenBecause it's not just the doctor. It's the whole ecology of care, the architecture, the noise level, the sense
54:5554 Minuten, 55 Sekundenof order or chaos, whether you feel safe or surveiled, whether the space communicates competence or neglect.
55:0355 Minuten, 3 SekundenThere's a body of research, much of it coming from environmental psychology and healthcare design showing that features
55:1055 Minuten, 10 Sekundenof the physical environment, natural light, views of greenery, reduced noise, single patient rooms correlate with

55:2755 Minuten, 27 Sekundenpublished a famous study back in 1984 showing that surgical patients whose hospital windows faced trees recovered
55:3555 Minuten, 35 Sekundenfaster and needed fewer painkillers than patients whose windows faced a brick wall. Same surgery, same surgeons, same
55:4355 Minuten, 43 Sekundendrugs, different view, different recovery.
55:4755 Minuten, 47 SekundenNow, is that a placebo effect? It depends on how loosely you want to use the term. It's not a sugar pill, but it
55:5555 Minuten, 55 Sekundenis the body responding to contextual cues, to signals from the environment that something is safe, that recovery is
56:0256 Minuten, 2 Sekundenpossible, that the situation is under control, and that response has measurable physiological consequences,
56:0956 Minuten, 9 Sekundencortisol drops, sleep improves, immune function ticks upward.
56:1556 Minuten, 15 Sekundenthe boundary between real medicine and everything around real medicine starts to look less like a wall and more like a
56:2456 Minuten, 24 Sekundengradient. And this is the part that's genuinely hard to hold in your head because it cuts against the clean
56:3156 Minuten, 31 Sekundencategories we like to use. We want medicine to be the pill, the procedure, the thing with the evidence base and the
56:3956 Minuten, 39 Sekundenregulatory approval. And it is those things, but it's also inescapably a performance. Not in the sense of being
56:4756 Minuten, 47 Sekundenfake, but in the theatrical sense, in the sense that medicine is enacted, staged, delivered in a context that
56:5556 Minuten, 55 Sekundenshapes its effects. The white coat is a costume. The stethoscope is a prop. The examination room is a set. And none of
57:0357 Minuten, 3 Sekundenthat makes the medicine less real. It makes it more complicated. It means that the effectiveness of a treatment is not
57:1157 Minuten, 11 Sekundena fixed property of the treatment itself but a variable property of the treatment in context. Change the context, change the outcome.
Kapitel 13: Evidence-based context
57:2157 Minuten, 21 SekundenBenadeti has a phrase for this that I find quietly brilliant. He talks about the psychosocial context of treatment
57:2957 Minuten, 29 Sekundenand he insists that this context is not a confound to be controlled for but a variable to be understood and where possible optimized.
57:4057 Minuten, 40 SekundenMost of clinical research is designed to subtract the context to isolate the specific effect of the molecule by
57:4757 Minuten, 47 Sekundencomparing it against a placebo that mimics everything except the active ingredient.
57:5357 Minuten, 53 SekundenAnd that's a perfectly valid thing to do. If your question is, "Does this molecule work, but it's not the only
58:0058 Minutenquestion. There's another question equally valid and far less often asked, which is how much of the healing that
58:0958 Minuten, 9 Sekundenhappens in this clinical encounter is coming from the molecule and how much is coming from everything else." And when
58:1858 Minuten, 18 Sekundenyou start asking that question seriously, the answers are uncomfortable for a lot of people genuinely uncomfortable
58:2658 Minuten, 26 Sekundenbecause the answers suggest that the context, the everything else is doing more work than we thought and in some cases more work than the molecule.
58:3858 Minuten, 38 SekundenLet me give you a concrete example of how someone tried to measure this.
58:4258 Minuten, 42 SekundenBenadeti, the same researcher who showed that hidden morphine is less effective than visible morphine, took the logic further.
58:5158 Minuten, 51 SekundenHe and his colleagues looked at a range of common medical treatments and asked a deceptively simple question. If you give
58:5958 Minuten, 59 Sekundensomeone a painkiller, but you remove every contextual cue that a painkiller has been given. No doctor walking in, no
59:0759 Minuten, 7 Sekundensyringe being prepared, no moment of this should start helping in a few minutes, just a computer controlled
59:1459 Minuten, 14 Sekundeninfusion dripping quietly into an IV line while the patient has no idea anything has changed. How much of the drug's effect survives?
59:2459 Minuten, 24 SekundenAnd the answer across multiple studies was that a meaningful portion of the drug's analesic power simply vanished.
59:3359 Minuten, 33 SekundenNot all of it. The molecule still did something. Morphine is morphine. It binds to opioid receptors regardless of
59:4159 Minuten, 41 Sekundenwhether you know it's there. But the size of the effect shrank. In some cases, it shrank by roughly a third. In
59:5059 Minuten, 50 Sekundenothers, by closer to half. The drug worked, but it worked less. And the missing portion, the gap between the
59:5959 Minuten, 59 Sekundenhidden dose and the open dose, that gap is the context.
1:00:051 Stunde, 5 SekundenThat's the part being supplied by expectation, by the ritual of treatment, by the patients belief that help is arriving.
1:00:141 Stunde, 14 SekundenThink about what that means for a second. It means that when your doctor hands you a pill and says, "This should
1:00:221 Stunde, 22 Sekundenhelp with the pain and you take it and 20 minutes later you feel better." Some of what you're feeling is the
1:00:291 Stunde, 29 Sekundenpharmarmacology and some of what you're feeling is the moment the doctor handed it to you. The two are tangled together
1:00:361 Stunde, 36 Sekundenin the actual experience of relief. And separating them cleanly is almost impossible outside a very controlled laboratory setting.
1:00:471 Stunde, 47 SekundenIn real life, you never get the molecule without the context. You always get both.
1:00:551 Stunde, 55 SekundenNow, this creates an interesting problem for how we evaluate treatments. The gold standard of medical evidence, the
1:01:021 Stunde, 1 Minute, 2 Sekundenrandomized controlled trial is specifically designed to subtract the context. You give half the patients the
1:01:111 Stunde, 1 Minute, 11 Sekundenreal drug and half the patients a sugar pill and both groups get the same white coat, the same examination, the same hopeful instructions.
1:01:221 Stunde, 1 Minute, 22 SekundenWhatever improvement the drug group shows over the placebo group, that's your specific effect. That's what the
1:01:291 Stunde, 1 Minute, 29 Sekundenmolecule is doing above and beyond the theater. And that number is what gets printed on the label, what gets
1:01:371 Stunde, 1 Minute, 37 Sekundensubmitted to the regulators, what determines whether the drug is approved.
1:01:431 Stunde, 1 Minute, 43 SekundenIt's a clean, elegant system, and it has saved countless lives by weeding out treatments that don't work.
1:01:511 Stunde, 1 Minute, 51 SekundenBut here's the thing, that system was built to answer one question. Does the molecule outperform a
1:01:591 Stunde, 1 Minute, 59 Sekundenblank? and it answers that question beautifully.
1:02:041 Stunde, 2 Minuten, 4 SekundenWhat it doesn't answer, what it wasn't designed to answer is how much total healing is happening in the room and where it's all coming from.
1:02:141 Stunde, 2 Minuten, 14 SekundenThe placebo group in a clinical trial isn't a nothing group.
1:02:191 Stunde, 2 Minuten, 19 SekundenThose people are getting examined, monitored, listened to, given a pill to take on a schedule, told they might be receiving a promising new treatment.
1:02:291 Stunde, 2 Minuten, 29 SekundenThey're embedded in a rich therapeutic context and as we've been talking about all evening that context has physiological consequences.
1:02:391 Stunde, 2 Minuten, 39 SekundenSo when a drug trial shows that the drug beat placebo by say 15% that doesn't mean the drug is
1:02:481 Stunde, 2 Minuten, 48 Sekundenresponsible for all the improvement in the drug group. It means the drug added 15 percentage points on top of whatever
1:02:551 Stunde, 2 Minuten, 55 Sekundenthe context was already doing. and the context might have been doing quite a lot. This is something that a Danish
1:03:031 Stunde, 3 Minuten, 3 Sekundenresearcher named Osborne Robartson who we talked about earlier, the one who challenged Beecher's original 35% claim,
1:03:121 Stunde, 3 Minuten, 12 Sekundenhas spent years thinking carefully about.
1:03:161 Stunde, 3 Minuten, 16 SekundenHerobiartson's position is nuanced and worth sitting with. He's skeptical of grand claims about placebo power and
1:03:241 Stunde, 3 Minuten, 24 Sekundenrightly so. He showed that when you compare placebo treatment against no treatment at all, the placebo effect is
1:03:321 Stunde, 3 Minuten, 32 Sekundenoften modest and mostly limited to subjective outcomes like pain and nausea rather than hard biological end points.
1:03:411 Stunde, 3 Minuten, 41 SekundenBut even doesn't deny that context matters. His point is more precise than that. His point is that we should be
1:03:501 Stunde, 3 Minuten, 50 Sekundencareful about what we attribute to placebo and what we attribute to other things.

1:04:521 Stunde, 4 Minuten, 52 Sekundenagain a week later, it will probably be lower, not because anything you did helped, but because extreme values tend
1:05:001 Stunde, 5 Minutento drift back toward the average. This is basic statistics, not healing. And a

1:05:271 Stunde, 5 Minuten, 27 SekundenSome of it is regression to the mean.
1:05:301 Stunde, 5 Minuten, 30 SekundenSome of it is reporting bias, the human tendency to tell the nice researcher that yes, you do feel a bit better

1:06:011 Stunde, 6 Minuten, 1 Sekundefiguring out how much of each, and that's extraordinarily difficult to do.
1:06:061 Stunde, 6 Minuten, 6 SekundenOne approach that researchers have used is the three arm trial. Instead of the usual two groups, drug versus placebo,
1:06:161 Stunde, 6 Minuten, 16 Sekundenyou add a third group that gets no treatment at all. They're on a waiting list or they receive standard care or
1:06:231 Stunde, 6 Minuten, 23 Sekundenthey simply come in for assessments without any intervention.
1:06:281 Stunde, 6 Minuten, 28 SekundenThis third group is your baseline. They show you what natural recovery and regression to the mean look like on
1:06:361 Stunde, 6 Minuten, 36 Sekundentheir own without any therapeutic context.
1:06:401 Stunde, 6 Minuten, 40 SekundenThen you can compare the placebo group against this no treatment group. And whatever difference you see that's closer to the true contextual effect.
1:06:501 Stunde, 6 Minuten, 50 SekundenIt's not perfect. Nothing in this field is perfect. But it gives you a much cleaner picture than the standard two
1:06:571 Stunde, 6 Minuten, 57 Sekundenarm design. And when researchers have done this, the results are interesting.
1:07:041 Stunde, 7 Minuten, 4 SekundenFor subjective outcomes, especially pain, the placebo group often does meaningfully better than the no

1:07:481 Stunde, 7 Minuten, 48 SekundenWhich makes sense, right?

1:08:041 Stunde, 8 Minuten, 4 SekundenThese are all experiences that the brain constructs and that the brain can within limits dial up or down. The brain is not

withdraw the entirety of their account which caused the entire system to crumble. Banks make money by lending
40:46
your money at a higher interest rate than they are giving you. That's really it. You're the supply of money and the
40:51

40:57
easier and more convenient to spend on a card or transfer than carrying around cash all the time. They are literally
41:02
paying you to hold your money with them in the form of interest. It is much safer to keep your money in a bank than in a shoe box in your room. In the US,
41:09
most banks are insured up to $250,000 per person, meaning no matter what, the government assures you that your money
41:15
up to 250K is safe. Interest. Imagine you borrow $1,000. You have to pay back
41:22
$1,280. Why? Because of interest. Interest is money's way of charging rent to exist in
41:28
someone else's hands. When you borrow, interest is the price tag for using someone else's cash. When you lend or
41:35
save, interest is the reward for being patient and boring. There are two main types. Simple interest is like, "Here's
41:41
a flat fee. Thanks for playing." Compound interest is every dollar I gave you now has clones and they also want
41:47
rent. Let's say you owe 20% interest on a credit card. You miss a payment. Now your interest is earning interest. Soon
41:54
your $12 burrito turns into a $50 regret. On the flip side, investing at 7% annual compound interest. That's your
42:01
money duplicating itself like a cheat code. $100 becomes $200, then $400, then
42:07
one day you wake up and you're old, rich, and a little smug about it. This is why interest is the silent engine
42:13
behind both wealth and debt. In loans, it's the slow burn that turns small mistakes into financial fires. In
42:19
investments, it's the time bomb that turns small gains into massive wins. So, what's the hack? If you're paying
42:26
interest, kill it fast. If you're earning interest, let it sit, feed it, and give it time. Interest is either
42:32
your worst enemy or your best unpaid employee. The choice is in who's collecting it. Inflation. Okay, so you
42:38
bought a bag of chips, open it up, and it looks like it's already been halfeaten. You check what you paid, 30%
42:45
higher than last time. Then you realize you've just been hit by inflation. Inflation is what happens when money
42:51
slowly gets less valuable over time. Not overnight, not with fireworks, just a
42:57
slow erosion. Your $5 bill still technically $5, but it buys less instant
43:02
noodles, less gas, and doesn't actually have as much value as it did before. So,
43:07
what actually causes it? Sometimes people just have too much money. Everyone's got cash, and they all want
43:13
to spend it on the same stuff. Let's say 2,000 people want this $500 TV, but the
43:18
business only has 1,000 TVs for sale. So, the business goes, "Oh, everyone wants this TV. That'll be $800." Now,
43:25
sometimes it's supply chains with hiccups or problems, making the cost of producing a good or service more
43:30
expensive, meaning the cost of that good or service must rise or sometimes just cause. Expectations can cause inflation.
43:37
If people think prices are rising, they'll spend more now, driving prices up faster. It's a self-fulfilling
43:43
economic prophecy. A little inflation is normal, even good. 2% a year, that's fine, predictable. But if it spikes,
43:50
savings die, wages lag. The government tries to fight inflation when this occurs by raising interest rates. When
43:57
the government raises interest rates, people are paying more interest or it's more expensive to get a loan, meaning
44:03
they have less money to spend on things like TVs. This causes a reduction in the amount of spending, pretty much cooling
44:09
off the economy. Recessions. A recession is when the economy decreases for at least two quarters or 6 months in simple
44:16
terms. One day you're fine, you've got a job, bills are paid, you might even be planning a trip with the family. But
44:22
suddenly there's layoffs, the stock markets only going down. In a recession,
44:28

44:34

44:45

 Aufrufe  
08.10.2026  heute-journal | Der Podcast
Der Bundesnachrichtendienst hat diese Woche für viele Schlagzeilen gesorgt. Zum einen durch die drastische Warnung vor Russland. Es führe „einen Schattenkrieg gegen uns“, so BND-Chef Martin Jäger.  

Zum anderen wurde der frühere BND-Chef August Hanning festgenommen. Die Bundesanwaltschaft wirft ihm versuchten Landesverrat und geheimdienstliche Agententätigkeit vor. 

Helene Reiner und Christian Sievers fragen in dieser Folge, wie der BND arbeitet und warum er immer wieder mit Skandalen in die Schlagzeilen gerät. Sie sprechen darüber, ob der Geheimdienst mehr Befugnisse braucht und sie klären, was hinter dem Begriff „Schattenkrieg“ steckt. 

Darüber sprechen sie mit Nico Lange vom Institut für Risikoanalysen und Internationale Sicherheit und mit dem Geheimdienstexperten Luca Manns von der Forschungsstelle Nachrichtendienste der Uni Köln.

heute journal - der Podcast – in der ZDF heute App, im Web und auf Youtube. 
Lasst gern eine Bewertung da und abonniert unseren Podcast. 
Wir freuen uns über Fragen, Kritik oder Themenvorschläge an: heutejournal-podcast@zdf.de

Hier auf ZDFheute Nachrichten erfahrt ihr, was auf der Welt passiert und was uns alle etwas angeht: Wir sorgen für Durchblick in der Nachrichtenwelt, erklären die Hintergründe und gehen auf gesellschaftliche Debatten ein. Diskutiert in Livestreams mit uns und bildet euch eure eigene Meinung mit den Fakten, die wir euch präsentieren.

Abonniert unseren Kanal, um nichts mehr zu verpassen.
Immer auf dem aktuellen Stand seid ihr auf https://www.ZDFheute.de/.

 Aufrufe  
09.10.2026
Now streaming on Spotify
https://open.spotify.com/show/033FF4Y...

Does the language you speak actually change the way you think, perceive reality, and understand the world?

This video explores the fascinating relationship between language and thought — from the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis and linguistic relativity to the ways different languages describe colors, time, space, emotions, and everyday experiences. We look at whether language simply expresses our thoughts or can also influence how our minds organize and interpret information.

We also explore how bilingualism affects cognitive processing, why some languages categorize the world differently, and what psychological experiments reveal about the relationship between words, perception, memory, and reasoning. Along the way, we examine the limits of linguistic relativity and why language may influence certain aspects of thinking without completely determining what we can understand.

A slow journey through linguistics, psychology, neuroscience, and the surprising connections between the words we use and the way we experience reality.

Resources:

Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Linguistic Relativity
https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/re...

Encyclopaedia Britannica — Sapir-Whorf Hypothesis
https://www.britannica.com/science/Sa...

American Psychological Association — APA Dictionary of Psychology
https://dictionary.apa.org/

https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/la...

Kapitel 1: The mystery of language
0:000 SekundenLet me ask you something.
0:022 SekundenHave you ever tried to describe a color to someone, a very specific color, and realized you didn't have a word for it?
0:1111 SekundenMaybe it was that particular shade of blue green you see in shallow ocean water when the sun hits the sand underneath. You know the color. You can
0:2020 Sekundenpicture it right now. But when you reach for a word, you kind of fumble around.

0:4141 Sekundenchange whether you can see it? Can you still perceive the difference between that shade and say the blue of a clear
0:4949 Sekundenwinter sky? Of course you can. Your eyes work just fine.
0:5454 SekundenBut, and this is the part that gets interesting.
0:5959 SekundenDoes not having that word make it just a tiny bit harder to remember the color later to think about it when it's not in
1:061 Minute, 6 Sekundenfront of you? To communicate it quickly and efficiently to someone else?
1:121 Minute, 12 SekundenAnd if so, does that mean the language you speak is quietly, subtly, almost invisibly shaping the way your mind works?
1:211 Minute, 21 SekundenThat question in various forms has haunted philosophers, linguists, psychologists, and even engineers for
1:291 Minute, 29 Sekundenwell over a century. And tonight, we're going to wander through the whole story of it slowly. There's no rush. If you
1:381 Minute, 38 Sekundendrift off somewhere along the way, that's perfectly fine.

Kapitel 2: Philosophical foundations
1:531 Minute, 53 SekundenSo, let's start at the beginning. Not the scientific beginning. We'll get there, but the philosophical beginning, which goes back surprisingly far.
2:032 Minuten, 3 SekundenBecause people have been wondering about the relationship between language and thought for a very, very long time.
2:092 Minuten, 9 SekundenThink about the ancient Greeks for a second. The word they used for reason, for rational thought, was logos.
2:172 Minuten, 17 SekundenBut logos also meant word or speech. The same term covered both concepts. To the Greeks, thinking and speaking were so

2:562 Minuten, 56 SekundenFor Aristotle, you couldn't really pull them apart.
3:003 MinutenLanguage wasn't just a tool you used to express your thoughts after you'd already had them. It was somehow part of the thinking itself.

3:273 Minuten, 27 Sekundeneventually spark decades of scientific research and controversy started taking shape in the late 1700s and early 1800s in Germany.
3:393 Minuten, 39 SekundenAnd it started with a man named Vilhelm Fon Humbult. Humbult is one of those figures who was into everything. His

4:094 Minuten, 9 SekundenAnd in his spare time, if you can call it that, he studied languages the way some people collect rare books. He threw

4:284 Minuten, 28 Sekundenover was how profoundly different these languages were from each other. Not just in their words, but in their structures.
4:374 Minuten, 37 SekundenThe way they organized reality into categories.
4:414 Minuten, 41 SekundenThe way they forced speakers to pay attention to certain things and ignore others.
4:474 Minuten, 47 SekundenHere's what Humbult came to believe, and I want you to hear this carefully because it's the seed of everything that comes later.
4:554 Minuten, 55 SekundenHe argued that language is not merely a vehicle for expressing thought.
5:015 Minuten, 1 SekundeLanguage, he said, is the formative organ of thought. That's his phrase, the formative organ. Meaning, language
5:095 Minuten, 9 Sekundendoesn't just carry your ideas from your brain to someone else's ears. It actually shapes those ideas in the first
5:175 Minuten, 17 Sekundenplace. Each language, he believed, contains within it a particular worldview.
5:245 Minuten, 24 Sekundenof Elton Shaolong to use the German term that's so perfect it got borrowed into English

5:505 Minuten, 50 Sekundenspeaks Mandarin and a person who speaks Navajo and a person who speaks Finnish aren't
5:575 Minuten, 57 Sekundenjust using different sounds to describe the same reality.
6:026 Minuten, 2 SekundenThey're actually experiencing subtly different realities.
6:066 Minuten, 6 SekundenTheir languages are carving up the world in different ways, highlighting different features, grouping things into different categories.
6:156 Minuten, 15 SekundenAnd those differences aren't trivial or superficial. They go deep. They affect how you perceive time, space, color,
6:256 Minuten, 25 Sekundencausality, relationships between objects, the whole architecture of your inner mental life. Now, that's a pretty
6:336 Minuten, 33 Sekundenbold claim. And in Humboldt's day, it was more of a philosophical intuition than a testable hypothesis.
6:416 Minuten, 41 SekundenHe didn't have the tools to prove it. He couldn't run experiments.
6:466 Minuten, 46 SekundenHe was working from his extraordinary knowledge of languages and his deep conviction that the differences he saw between them mattered in some
6:546 Minuten, 54 Sekundenfundamental way. But the idea didn't die with him. It traveled. It traveled in particular to the United States and it
Kapitel 3: Boas and cultural relativism
7:037 Minuten, 3 Sekundenlanded in the mind of a man named France Boas.
7:087 Minuten, 8 SekundenBoas is sometimes called the father of American anthropology and that title is welld deserved.
7:157 Minuten, 15 SekundenBorn in Germany in 1858, he trained originally as a physicist, then became fascinated by geography and then on a
7:247 Minuten, 24 Sekundenresearch expedition to Baffan Island in the Canadian Arctic in 1883.
7:307 Minuten, 30 SekundenHe fell in love with the study of human cultures. He spent time with the Inuit people there, learned their language,
7:377 Minuten, 37 Sekundenand came back a changed man. He eventually settled in America, took a position at Columbia University in New
7:457 Minuten, 45 SekundenYork, and proceeded to reshape the entire field of anthropology over the next four decades.
7:537 Minuten, 53 SekundenHere's what matters about Boaz for our story.
7:577 Minuten, 57 SekundenHe was one of the first serious scientists to insist that you could not understand a culture without understanding its language. And you
8:068 Minuten, 6 Sekundencould not understand a language without doing deep, careful, respectful fieldwork with the people who actually
8:148 Minuten, 14 Sekundenspoke it. He sent his students out to live with indigenous communities across North America to learn their languages
8:228 Minuten, 22 Sekundenfrom scratch to document grammar and vocabulary with painstaking precision.
8:288 Minuten, 28 SekundenAnd what those students found again and again was that these languages were not simplified or primitive versions of European languages.
8:388 Minuten, 38 SekundenThey were extraordinarily complex, often in ways that European languages were not. They made distinctions that English
8:478 Minuten, 47 Sekundenor French or German simply didn't bother with, and they left unmarked things that European languages treated as essential.
8:568 Minuten, 56 SekundenBoaz himself made a famous observation about Inuit words for snow.
9:029 Minuten, 2 SekundenNow, I should pause here because you've probably heard some version of this.
9:089 Minuten, 8 SekundenIt's become one of those factoids that floats around popular culture, sometimes exaggerated to absurd levels. The
9:169 Minuten, 16 SekundenEskimos have 50 words for snow or 100 words or 200.
9:229 Minuten, 22 SekundenThe reality is more nuanced and more interesting than the myth. What Boas actually pointed out in his 1911
9:319 Minuten, 31 Sekundenhandbook of American Indian languages was that the Inuit language uses different root words for different types
9:389 Minuten, 38 Sekundenof snow. falling snow, snow on the ground, drifting snow, packed snow,
9:469 Minuten, 46 Sekundenwhere English uses the single word snow and then adds modifiers.
9:519 Minuten, 51 SekundenIt wasn't that Inuit speakers had some magical snow perception that English speakers lacked. It was that their
9:589 Minuten, 58 Sekundenlanguage encoded snow distinctions at a deeper grammatical level.
10:0310 Minuten, 3 SekundenAnd Boas used this as an example of how different languages categorize experience differently. But Boas himself
10:1210 Minuten, 12 Sekundenwas actually pretty cautious about drawing strong conclusions from this. He didn't claim that Inuit speakers thought differently because of their language.
10:2210 Minuten, 22 SekundenHe was more interested in showing that all languages were equally complex and sophisticated, just in different ways.
10:3010 Minuten, 30 SekundenHe was fighting against the racism of his era.
10:3310 Minuten, 33 Sekundenagainst the widespread assumption that primitive peoples had primitive languages and therefore primitive minds.
10:4210 Minuten, 42 SekundenHis point was the opposite. Every human language is a marvel of complexity. And the differences between languages tell
10:5010 Minuten, 50 Sekundenus about cultural priorities and environments, not about the intelligence of their speakers. It was Boas's students who
Kapitel 4: Sapir and linguistic habits
10:5810 Minuten, 58 Sekundenwould push the idea further. And the most important of those students for our purposes was a man named Edward Sappir.
11:0911 Minuten, 9 SekundenSappir was born in 1884 in what is now Germany, grew up in New York City, and studied under Boas at Colombia. He was

11:3411 Minuten, 34 Sekundenand many others. He documented languages that were even then on the verge of disappearing.
11:4211 Minuten, 42 SekundenAnd as he worked, he developed a deep conviction that language and thought were intimately connected.
11:4911 Minuten, 49 SekundenSpir wrote something in 1929 that would become one of the most quoted passages in the history of linguistics. He said
11:5711 Minuten, 57 Sekundenthat human beings do not live in the objective world alone but are very much at the mercy of the particular language which has become the medium of
12:0512 Minuten, 5 Sekundenexpression for their society. He said that the real world is to a large extent unconsciously built upon the language
12:1412 Minuten, 14 Sekundenhabits of the group. And then the line that really sticks, we see and hear and
12:2112 Minuten, 21 Sekundenotherwise experience very largely as we do because the language habits of our community predispose certain choices of interpretation.
12:3112 Minuten, 31 SekundenRead that again in your mind. We experience largely as we do because of our language habits.
12:3912 Minuten, 39 SekundenThat's not just saying language influences how we talk about our experiences.
12:4412 Minuten, 44 SekundenIt's saying language influences the experiences themselves, the seeing, the
12:5012 Minuten, 50 Sekundenhearing, the raw perception. That's a strong claim. And Sappir knew it was a strong claim, but he believed the
12:5912 Minuten, 59 Sekundenevidence from his decades of fieldwork supported it. Now, Sappir was a careful, rigorous scholar. He published his ideas
13:0713 Minuten, 7 Sekundenin academic contexts, hedged them appropriately, and acknowledged their complexity.
13:1413 Minuten, 14 SekundenBut he also had a student. And this student would take these ideas and push them further than Sappir himself might have been comfortable with into
13:2213 Minuten, 22 Sekundenterritory that was bolder, more provocative, and ultimately more controversial than anything Spir had
13:3013 Minuten, 30 Sekundenwritten. This student's name was Benjamin Lee Horf. And his story is one of the strangest and most fascinating in
Kapitel 5: Whorf's bold time claim
13:3813 Minuten, 38 Sekundenthe entire history of science. Because Benjamin Lee Horf was not a professional linguist. He wasn't a professor. He didn't have a PhD.
13:4913 Minuten, 49 SekundenBy day, he worked as a fire prevention inspector for the Hartford Fire Insurance Company in Connecticut. And the way he got into linguistics in the
13:5813 Minuten, 58 Sekundenfirst place, the thing that set him on the path to becoming one of the most debated thinkers of the 20th century
14:0514 Minuten, 5 Sekundenstarted with fire. Literal fire. the kind that burns buildings down.
14:1214 Minuten, 12 SekundenHorf noticed something in his insurance work that fascinated him. He noticed that the language people used to
14:1914 Minuten, 19 Sekundendescribe situations affected how they behaved around those situations. His most famous example involved gasoline
14:2714 Minuten, 27 Sekundendrums. When workers were around drums labeled gasoline, they were careful. No
14:3414 Minuten, 34 Sekundensmoking, no open flames, cautious behavior. But when they were around drums labeled empty gasoline drums, they
14:4214 Minuten, 42 Sekundenrelaxed. They'd smoke nearby, toss cigarette butts around. And here's the thing, those empty drums were often more
14:5114 Minuten, 51 Sekundendangerous than the full ones because they were full of explosive vapor. The word empty made people think safe, even
15:0015 Minutenthough the physical reality was the opposite of safe. The label, the language was overriding their assessment
15:0815 Minuten, 8 Sekundenof the actual danger. That observation lit something up in Horf's mind. He started wondering if a single word like
15:1715 Minuten, 17 Sekundenempty could reshape how people perceived risk in such a concrete life or death way. What might entire language systems
15:2615 Minuten, 26 Sekundenbe doing to the way their speakers perceived everything? And that question led him in the early 1930s to start studying linguistics seriously.
15:3615 Minuten, 36 SekundenHe enrolled in Edward Spir's courses at Yale and he threw himself into the study of indigenous American languages,
15:4415 Minuten, 44 Sekundenparticularly Hopi, the language spoken by the Hopi people of northeastern Arizona.
15:5015 Minuten, 50 SekundenAnd what he found in Hopi or what he believed he found would become the most famous and most controversial claim in
15:5715 Minuten, 57 Sekundenthe entire debate about language and thought. It had to do with something so fundamental to human experience that you
16:0516 Minuten, 5 Sekundenprobably never even think about whether it could vary from one person to another. It had to do with time. The way we experience time itself.
16:1516 Minuten, 15 SekundenNow think about that for a second. Time feels like one of those bedrock things, right? It's just
16:2516 Minuten, 25 Sekundenthere. It moves forward. The past is behind you. The future is ahead of you.
16:3216 Minuten, 32 SekundenAnd the present is this thin little edge you're always standing on. That's not a cultural idea. That's just how time
16:3916 Minuten, 39 Sekundenworks. Or at least that's what most of us assume. But Horf looked at Hopi and said, "Actually, no." He claimed that
16:4916 Minuten, 49 Sekundenthe Hopi language didn't treat time the way European languages do. He argued that Hopi had no words, no grammatical
16:5716 Minuten, 57 Sekundenforms, no constructions that referred to time as a flowing linear thing, as something you could divide into neat
17:0617 Minuten, 6 Sekundenchunks of past, present, and future, the way English does, the way French does,
17:1217 Minuten, 12 Sekundenthe way German does. And that's a pretty staggering claim when you sit with it.
Kapitel 6: Whorfian controversy
17:1917 Minuten, 19 SekundenBecause what Horf was really saying wasn't just that hopy people used different words for time. He was saying
17:2717 Minuten, 27 Sekundenthat the structure of their language encoded a fundamentally different relationship with temporal experience.
17:3617 Minuten, 36 SekundenWhere English speakers naturally think of time as a kind of river flowing past them. Yesterday upstream, tomorrow
17:4417 Minuten, 44 Sekundendownstream. Warf argued that Hopy speakers experienced something more like a distinction between what is manifest,
17:5317 Minuten, 53 Sekundenwhat is already realized in the world, and what is manifesting, what is in the process of becoming.

Kapitel 17: The cost of language loss
1:42:311 Stunde, 42 Minuten, 31 SekundenWhich brings us to a question that's been gaining urgency in recent years.
1:42:361 Stunde, 42 Minuten, 36 SekundenAnd it's not just an academic question anymore. It's a question with real consequences for education, for policy,
1:42:441 Stunde, 42 Minuten, 44 Sekundenfor technology, for how we think about artificial intelligence and the future of human communication.
1:42:511 Stunde, 42 Minuten, 51 SekundenAnd that question is if language shapes thought in all these ways we've been talking about through color perception,
1:43:001 Stunde, 43 Minutenspatial reasoning, numerical cognition, emotional granularity, moral judgment, memory for events. Then what happens when languages die?
1:43:111 Stunde, 43 Minuten, 11 SekundenBecause languages are dying, they're dying at an extraordinary rate, linguists estimate that of the roughly
1:43:181 Stunde, 43 Minuten, 18 Sekunden7,000 languages spoken on Earth today, somewhere between a third and a half will fall silent by the end of this
1:43:251 Stunde, 43 Minuten, 25 Sekundencentury. That's a language going extinct roughly every 2 weeks. And each one of those languages represents not just a

1:43:521 Stunde, 43 Minuten, 52 Sekundentraining the mind along particular paths.

1:44:041 Stunde, 44 Minuten, 4 SekundenWe lose the perceptual distinctions they sharpen, the conceptual categories they maintain, the reasoning patterns they
1:44:121 Stunde, 44 Minuten, 12 Sekundenencourage. We lose ways of thinking that no one will ever think again. And unlike a building or a painting, you can't put
1:44:211 Stunde, 44 Minuten, 21 Sekundena dead language in a museum and preserve what it did to the minds of its speakers. The cognitive effects are
1:44:281 Stunde, 44 Minuten, 28 Sekundenalive only as long as the language is alive, being spoken, being heard, being used to think with.

How does your body actually feel pain, and why can the same sensation feel completely different from one person to another?

This video explores the fascinating science of pain — from specialized sensory receptors and nerve signals to the spinal cord and brain networks that ultimately create the experience of pain. We look at what happens when tissue is damaged, how pain signals travel through the nervous system, and why pain is much more complicated than a simple warning from the body.

We also explore acute and chronic pain, pain thresholds, inflammation, pain modulation, phantom limb pain, and the surprising ways that emotions, attention, expectations, and past experiences can influence how strongly something hurts.

A slow journey through nerves, the spinal cord, the brain, and the complex biological processes behind one of the body’s most important protective systems.

measurably change their pain outcomes. Laurammer Mosley, an Australian
1:47:44
neuroscientist and physiootherapist who's become one of the most influential voices in modern pain science, has built
1:47:51
an entire approach around this idea. His work on pain neuroscience education,
1:47:57
literally teaching patients about how pain works, explaining that pain doesn't equal damage, that the nervous system
1:48:04
can become oversensitive, that hurt doesn't always mean harm. has been shown
1:48:10
in multiple studies to reduce pain and improve function. Not because the education changes anything in the
1:48:16
tissues, but because it changes the brain's predictions. When you understand that your back pain
1:48:23
doesn't necessarily mean your spine is crumbling, the threat level drops. When
1:48:28
the threat level drops, the neuromatrix recalculates and the pain output can
1:48:34
decrease. This is extraordinary if you think about it. knowledge itself becomes a treatment.
1:48:42
Understanding the mechanism changes the mechanism. It's a kind of beautiful recursion. The system that generates
1:48:49
pain can be influenced by understanding how the system generates pain. And it
1:48:54
connects back to everything we've been talking about from gate control to the neuromatrix to central sensitization.
1:49:02
All of those discoveries were steps toward recognizing that pain is not a fixed signal traveling up a wire. It's a
1:49:09
dynamic, context dependent, modifiable experience constructed by a brain that's
1:49:15
trying, sometimes clumsily, sometimes brilliantly, to protect you. And that
1:49:21
recognition has practical consequences that extend far beyond the clinic. It's
1:49:26
reshaping how we think about things like workplace injury, disability assessment,
1:49:31
even legal definitions of suffering. For decades, the medical legal system operated on a biomed model. Find the
1:49:39
tissue damage, quantify it, assign a pain level. If imaging shows a herniated
1:49:45
disc, the pain is real. If imaging shows nothing, the pain is suspect. But we now
1:49:52
know that's deeply flawed. Imaging findings correlate poorly with pain.
1:49:58
Plenty of people with dramatic looking MR is have no pain at all and plenty of
1:50:03
people with clean scans are in agony. The tissue is not the whole story. It
1:50:08
never was. And yet changing institutional and cultural assumptions about pain is slow, difficult work.
1:50:17
Physicians trained in the biomedical model sometimes struggle to embrace the biocschosocial framework. not because
1:50:24
they're closed-minded, but because the new model is genuinely harder. It's
1:50:29
easier to point to a scan and prescribe a pill than to address someone's fear
1:50:35
avoidance beliefs, their sleep quality, their social isolation, their
1:50:40
catastrophizing patterns, their childhood trauma, and their neuroplastic
1:50:45
spinal cord changes all at once. The complexity is real and the systems
1:50:51
we've built, insurance reimbursement, clinical time constraints, specialist
1:50:57
silos, aren't designed for it. But the science keeps pushing forward.
1:51:04
And one of the most exciting frontiers right now involves something that would have seemed like science fiction to
1:51:10

1:51:16

1:51:21

1:51:28

1:51:34

1:51:41

1:51:46

1:51:53

1:51:58

1:52:03

1:52:08

1:52:14

1:52:22
event. And that's a big deal because one of the oldest frustrations in pain
1:52:28

1:52:36

1:52:43

1:52:49

1:52:54

1:53:01

1:53:08

1:53:16

1:53:23

1:53:29

1:53:36

1:53:41

1:53:48

1:53:55

1:54:03

1:54:08

1:54:15

1:54:21

1:54:28

1:54:34

1:54:40

1:54:46

1:55:18

1:55:24

1:55:29

1:55:37
